\title{\textbf{Engineering Reliable LLM-Based Data Analysis: An Empirical Study of Schema Grounding, Planning, Verification, and SQL Repair}}

\begin{abstract}
While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate notable code-generation capabilities, translating natural language questions into reliable analytical SQL over relational databases (Text-to-SQL) remains brittle in practice. In this paper, we investigate the empirical mechanisms governing Text-to-SQL reliability: \textbf{structural verification improves query reliability, whereas aggressive automated repair can introduce substantial semantic regressions}. We evaluate a multi-stage reliability pipeline on a frozen 500-query benchmark across 8 business domains over a public relational e-commerce data warehouse (the Olist dataset, 9 tables, 100,000+ orders). Our system achieves a \textbf{\HeadlineEquivalentAccuracy{} Result Equivalence Rate under the study comparator} (367/500 queries, 95\% Wilson Score CI: [\HeadlineEquivalentCILower{}, \HeadlineEquivalentCIUpper{}]), \textbf{\HeadlineExactMatchAccuracy{} Exact Match}, and \textbf{\HeadlineSQLExecutionSuccess{} SQL Execution Success} with a mean latency of \HeadlineMeanLatency{} ($p50$: \HeadlinePFiftyLatency{}, $p95$: \HeadlinePNinetyFiveLatency{}). In a controlled 4-way 100-query ablation, activating deterministic Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) structural verification significantly improves result equivalence over unverified planning (Config~C 26.0\% vs.\ Config~B 15.0\%, McNemar exact $p=0.0192$, $\text{Odds Ratio}=3.75$). However, an exhaustive audit of all \TotalRepairTriggered{} repair events reveals that automated self-repair is a double-edged mechanism: while 97 of 101 post-repair queries (96.0\%) were syntactically valid and preserved \RepairMaintainedCount{} already-correct queries, repair yielded only \RepairTrulyRecoveredCount{} genuine recoveries while inducing \RepairHarmedFalsePositiveCount{} harmful false-positive regressions. Furthermore, a cross-schema transfer probe across \SpiderUniqueDatabases{} external databases from the Spider benchmark demonstrates that while execution stability is preserved (100.0\%), result equivalence drops to \SpiderEquivalentAccuracy{} (9/50), highlighting the gap between in-domain grounding and zero-shot schema transfer. We conclude that conservative, uncertainty-aware structural verification is preferable to unconstrained automated repair loops.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction and Central Thesis}
Natural language interfaces to relational databases (Text-to-SQL) have received widespread attention for democratizing analytical access \cite{yu2018spider,li2023bird}. However, translating ambiguous business questions into sound SQL over normalized multi-table schemas reveals a fundamental operational reality:
\begin{center}
\textit{Executable SQL is not necessarily reliable analytical SQL.}
\end{center}
A query may compile cleanly and execute without database runtime exceptions, yet return corrupted figures due to systemic structural failure modes: schema hallucinations, join-path omissions, aggregation grain mismatches, and filter inconsistencies.

\paragraph{Central Thesis.}
Rather than presenting Text-to-SQL as an unconstrained agentic pipeline, this empirical study establishes that:
\begin{center}
\textbf{Deterministic structural verification improves Text-to-SQL reliability, while aggressive automated repair can introduce semantic regressions.}
\end{center}
Our evidence directly supports this thesis:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Verification Benefit:} In a controlled ablation, activating AST-based structural verification improves result equivalence from 15.0\% to 26.0\% over unverified planning (McNemar exact $p=0.0192$, $\text{OR}=3.75$).
    \item \textbf{Repair Hazard:} An audit of all 101 repair events reveals that compiler execution validity masks semantic degradation, producing \textbf{22 harmful false-positive regressions} against only \textbf{4 genuine recoveries}.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Research Questions and Summary of Findings}
To evaluate these mechanisms systematically, we address five explicit research questions:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{RQ1: Overall Reliability --- Does the multi-stage pipeline achieve high result equivalence on a complex data warehouse?} \\
    $\rightarrow$ \textbf{Answer:} On the 500-query benchmark across 8 domains, the system achieves \textbf{\HeadlineEquivalentAccuracy{} Result Equivalence} under the study comparator (95\% Wilson CI: [\HeadlineEquivalentCILower{}, \HeadlineEquivalentCIUpper{}]) and \textbf{\HeadlineSQLExecutionSuccess{} SQL Execution Success}.
    \item \textbf{RQ2: Verification Impact --- What is the marginal effect of deterministic AST structural verification?} \\
    $\rightarrow$ \textbf{Answer:} Adding AST structural verification significantly increases execution reliability from 34.0\% to 65.0\% and result equivalence from 15.0\% to 26.0\% (McNemar exact $p=0.0192$, $\text{OR}=3.75$).
    \item \textbf{RQ3: Repair Dynamics --- Does automated self-repair reliably fix broken queries without harming valid ones?} \\
    $\rightarrow$ \textbf{Answer:} No. While 96.0\% of post-repair queries execute cleanly and 49 correct queries are maintained, repair produced only \textbf{4 genuine recoveries} while causing \textbf{22 false-positive regressions}.
    \item \textbf{RQ4: Failure Taxonomy --- What structural failure modes dominate remaining non-equivalent queries?} \\
    $\rightarrow$ \textbf{Answer:} Among the 133 non-equivalent queries, failure is dominated by missing join paths (27.8\%), filter omissions/errors (24.8\%), and aggregation mismatches (24.1\%).
    \item \textbf{RQ5: Cross-Schema Transfer --- Does warehouse-grounded reliability transfer to unseen external schemas?} \\
    $\rightarrow$ \textbf{Answer:} Execution stability is fully preserved (100.0\%), but result equivalence drops to \textbf{18.0\%} (9/50) on a 20-database Spider transfer probe, exposing the gap between deep schema grounding and zero-shot transfer.
\end{itemize}

\section{Summary of Contributions}
We summarize our core contributions as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Controlled Empirical Decomposition:} We evaluate the marginal effect of deterministic AST verification over unverified planning, demonstrating a statistically significant reliability gain ($p=0.0192$).
    \item \textbf{Repair-Risk Characterization:} We present an exhaustive 4-way semantic audit of 101 repair events, showing that execution-valid repair can induce substantial false-positive regressions (22 harmed vs.\ 4 recovered).
    \item \textbf{Systematic Failure Taxonomy:} We categorize all 133 non-equivalent queries using AST diffing across six core structural failure classes.
    \item \textbf{Cross-Schema Transfer Probe:} We report zero-shot transfer evaluation across 20 unseen SQLite databases from the Spider benchmark, demonstrating execution robustness alongside a marked semantic generalization drop.
    \item \textbf{Audited Open Science Package:} We release all source code, frozen benchmark definitions, evaluation scripts, LaTeX manuscripts, and a cryptographic SHA-256 artifact manifest.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}
\paragraph{Text-to-SQL Benchmarks and Decomposition Methods.}
Benchmarks such as Spider \cite{yu2018spider} and BIRD \cite{li2023bird} evaluate LLMs on multi-table joins, nested subqueries, and execution accuracy. Decomposition frameworks such as DIN-SQL \cite{pourreza2023dinsql} and MAC-SQL \cite{wang2024macsql} show that dividing generation into sub-problems (schema linking, classification, SQL generation, correction) improves performance over monolithic prompting. Our work builds upon this paradigm by introducing deterministic, AST-level structural verification gates that inspect query structure prior to execution.

\paragraph{Schema Linking and Retrieval-Augmented Generation.}
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \cite{lewis2020rag,asai2023selfrag} grounds LLM generation in external knowledge. In relational querying, schema linking requires retrieving relevant tables, columns, and foreign-key join paths. While prior approaches rely primarily on dense embeddings or BM25 keyword matching, we evaluate hybrid retrieval augmented with explicit foreign-key graph traversal to preserve schema connectivity.

\paragraph{Agentic Architectures and Self-Correction Hazards.}
Iterative reasoning architectures such as ReAct \cite{yao2022react} and Reflexion \cite{shinn2023reflexion} leverage feedback loops for self-correction. In Text-to-SQL, execution-guided self-correction feeds compiler errors back to the LLM \cite{gao2023text2sql}. However, our empirical audit demonstrates that relying solely on execution feedback is hazardous: 96\% of post-repair queries execute cleanly without engine exceptions, yet over 21\% suffer from false-positive regressions that degrade previously correct queries.

\section{Reliability-Oriented System Architecture}
Our architecture decomposes analytical SQL synthesis into a 5-stage pipeline (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}):

\subsection{Graph-Guided Semantic Schema RAG}
Rather than passing an entire database schema into the LLM context, our retriever combines BM25 keyword matching, dense embedding retrieval via SentenceTransformers, and foreign-key graph traversal. Given a user query, the retriever extracts the minimal required schema subgraph, achieving \HeadlineTablePrecision{} macro precision and \HeadlineTableRecall{} macro recall across the 500-query benchmark.

\subsection{Structured DAG Query Planning \& Deterministic Plan Validation}
Before emitting SQL code, the planner synthesizes a structural JSON DAG declaring target metrics, grain dimensions, required tables, and explicit join paths. A deterministic \texttt{PlanValidator} statically inspects this DAG against the live database catalog, pruning hallucinated column references or invalid foreign-key joins prior to SQL generation.

\subsection{AST-Based SQL Structural Verification \& Closed-Loop Repair}
Generated SQL statements are parsed into Abstract Syntax Trees (AST) using SQLGlot \cite{sqlglot2023}. The \texttt{SQLSemanticVerifier} statically enforces:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Dialect Compliance:} Translating dialect-specific functions (\texttt{DATEDIFF}, \texttt{DATE\_TRUNC}) into canonical SQLite expressions (\texttt{strftime}, \texttt{julianday}).
    \item \textbf{Join Fan-Out \& Grain Integrity:} Verifying that non-aggregated projection columns appear in \texttt{GROUP BY} clauses and detecting cartesian products.
    \item \textbf{Canonical Metric Source Mapping:} Enforcing standardized column mappings (e.g., mapping revenue to \texttt{order\_items.price}).
\end{itemize}
When violations are identified, the verifier triggers targeted closed-loop repair prompts detailing the specific AST constraint violation.

\section{Experimental Methodology}

\subsection{Data Warehouse \& Benchmark Corpus}
We evaluate our system on an enterprise-style relational schema constructed from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset (Olist \cite{olist2018kaggle}):
\begin{itemize}\sloppy
    \item \textbf{9 Relational Tables:} \texttt{customers}, \texttt{orders}, \texttt{order\_items}, \texttt{order\_payments}, \texttt{order\_reviews}, \texttt{products}, \texttt{sellers}, \texttt{geolocation}, and \texttt{product\_category\_name\_translation}.
    \item \textbf{Scale:} 100,000+ customer orders, 112,650 order items, and 1,000,000+ geolocation points.
    \item \textbf{Benchmark Corpus:} A frozen 500-query benchmark dataset (\texttt{benchmark\_dataset\_500.json}) stratified across 8 business domains and 3 difficulty tiers (Easy: 114, Medium: 276, Hard: 110).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Evaluation Metrics \& Methodological Definitions}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Result Equivalence Rate under the Study Comparator (95\% Wilson CI):} Evaluates whether executed SQL results match ground-truth result sets under row-order invariance (comparing row multisets via item Counters) with numerical tolerance ($\epsilon=0.01$) and string whitespace normalization. Positional column semantics are preserved. We emphasize that result equivalence is an empirical evaluation criterion under the study comparator, not a generic classification accuracy or formal mathematical proof of semantic correctness.
    \item \textbf{Exact Match Rate:} Strict character-for-character equality of raw SQL output rows and column headers.
    \item \textbf{SQL Execution Success Rate:} Percentage of generated queries that execute without database engine runtime errors. Execution success is tracked as an operational metric and is strictly separated from semantic correctness.
    \item \textbf{Table Precision, Recall, and Exact Match:} Measuring table-retrieval alignment between generated and ground-truth queries.
\end{itemize}

\section{Controlled Component Ablation}
To measure the marginal impact of individual pipeline stages, we evaluated four controlled configurations across 100 identical benchmark query instances (Table~\ref{tab:phase_progression}):
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Config A (RAG Only):} Direct prompt-based generation from retrieved schema; verifier disabled.
    \item \textbf{Config B (RAG + Planner):} LLM DAG planner with plan validation; verifier disabled.
    \item \textbf{Config C (RAG + Planner + Verifier):} LLM DAG planner with AST structural verifier and repair active.
    \item \textbf{Config D (Full System):} Multi-stage pipeline including post-execution evaluator agent.
\end{itemize}

\IfFileExists{tables/tab_phase_progression.tex}{\input{tables/tab_phase_progression.tex}}{\input{../tables/tab_phase_progression.tex}}

\paragraph{Ablation Findings.}
Config~B (adding an unverified planner) causes execution success to collapse from 99.0\% to 34.0\% and result equivalence to drop from 19.0\% to 15.0\%, because unconstrained multi-step DAG planning introduces complex structural and alias errors. Activating the AST Structural Verifier (Config~C) substantially restores reliability: execution success rises from 34.0\% to 65.0\% (+31.0\%), and result equivalence improves from 15.0\% to 26.0\% (+11.0\%). 

In a matched paired McNemar test on the 100 identical queries, Config~C demonstrates a statistically significant improvement over Config~B (exact binomial $p=0.0192 < 0.05$, $\text{Odds Ratio}=3.75$, with 15 queries solved only by Config~C vs.\ 4 solved only by Config~B), establishing that AST-based structural verification significantly improves performance over unverified planning. However, this ablation does not establish that planning itself improves performance over direct RAG (Config~B 15.0\% vs.\ Config~A 19.0\%), nor does it prove that the full multi-stage architecture is causally superior.

\section{Granular Audit of the 101 Repair Cases}
To evaluate the true dynamics of automated self-repair, we conducted an exhaustive audit of all \TotalRepairTriggered{} repair events triggered during the 500-query benchmark run (Table~\ref{tab:repair_audit} and Figure~\ref{fig:repair}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\textwidth]{fig4_repair_dynamics.pdf}
\caption{Granular Audit of the 101 Repair Cases: Syntactic Validity Pipeline (Panel A) and Pre $\rightarrow$ Post Semantic Transitions (Panel B: 49 maintained, 26 remained incorrect, 22 harmed false positives, 4 truly recovered).}
\label{fig:repair}
\end{figure}

\IfFileExists{tables/tab_repair_audit.tex}{\input{tables/tab_repair_audit.tex}}{\input{../tables/tab_repair_audit.tex}}

\paragraph{Key Empirical Findings on Automated Repair:}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Execution Success Is Not Semantic Recovery:} While 97 of 101 post-repair queries (96.0\%) executed cleanly on SQLite, only 52.5\% (53/101) produced correct result sets. Describing compiler execution validity as repair recovery is methodologically invalid.
    \item \textbf{The False-Positive Regression Hazard:} Out of 101 triggered repair events, 71 queries were already semantically correct before repair was invoked. For \RepairHarmedFalsePositiveCount{} of these queries (21.8\% of all repair events), the automated repair agent degraded a correct query into an incorrect one (e.g., by injecting erroneous date filters or altering valid join aliases).
    \item \textbf{Genuine Recovery Rate:} Automated repair genuinely rescued only \RepairTrulyRecoveredCount{} previously broken queries (\texttt{q\_291}, \texttt{q\_346}, \texttt{q\_442}, \texttt{q\_476}), while preserving \RepairMaintainedCount{} already-correct queries and failing to resolve \RepairRemainedIncorrectCount{} incorrect queries.
\end{enumerate}
This finding represents a central empirical takeaway: unrestricted rule-based repair risks inducing substantial false-positive regressions, indicating that conservative, uncertainty-gated verification is preferable to unconstrained repair loops.

\section{AST Failure Taxonomy}
We analyzed all \TotalFailuresAnalyzed{} non-equivalent queries from the 500-query evaluation using AST diffing against ground-truth SQL (Figure~\ref{fig:taxonomy}):
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Schema Missing Join Path (37 queries, 27.8\% of errors / 7.4\% overall):} Omission of required intermediate bridging tables (e.g., joining \texttt{order\_reviews} to \texttt{customers} without traversing \texttt{orders}).
    \item \textbf{Semantic Filter Omission or Error (33 queries, 24.8\% of errors / 6.6\% overall):} Missing domain-specific predicates (e.g., omitting \texttt{order\_status = 'delivered'}) or filtering on incorrect timestamp fields.
    \item \textbf{Semantic Aggregation Mismatch (32 queries, 24.1\% of errors / 6.4\% overall):} Using incorrect aggregation functions (\texttt{AVG} instead of \texttt{SUM}) or inconsistent currency rounding.
    \item \textbf{Schema Hallucinated Table (15 queries, 11.3\% of errors / 3.0\% overall):} Synthesizing nonexistent subqueries or table aliases absent from the schema catalog.
    \item \textbf{Grain / GROUP BY Mismatch (14 queries, 10.5\% of errors / 2.8\% overall):} Grouping by string aliases rather than canonical date expressions, causing grain collision.
    \item \textbf{Semantic Ranking Order Mismatch (2 queries, 1.5\% of errors / 0.4\% overall):} Inverted \texttt{ASC}/\texttt{DESC} ordering or missing \texttt{ORDER BY} in ranking queries.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Controlled Synthetic Perturbation Robustness}
To examine sensitivity to controlled lexical and semantic shifts, we evaluated a deterministic 50-query synthetic perturbation suite ($N=50$, 10 queries per vector across 8 domains; Table~\ref{tab:robustness} and Figure~\ref{fig:robustness}). We emphasize that this suite tests specific local perturbation robustness rather than broad out-of-distribution or cross-domain generalization.

\IfFileExists{tables/tab_robustness.tex}{\input{tables/tab_robustness.tex}}{\input{../tables/tab_robustness.tex}}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\textwidth]{fig6_robustness_degradation.pdf}
\caption{Robustness under controlled synthetic perturbations ($N=50$ total; 10 queries per perturbation vector).}
\label{fig:robustness}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Robustness Observations.}
The pipeline demonstrates high retention under query paraphrasing (80.0\% retention), ranking phrasing variants (100.0\% retention), and synonym substitution (100.0\% retention). Temporal boundary shifts exhibit moderate degradation (85.7\% retention). However, character-level typographical noise causes severe degradation (57.1\% retention, 30.0\% absolute drop), exposing the vulnerability of exact token-matching in the schema retriever.

\section{Cross-Schema Transfer Evaluation}
To examine whether performance in a controlled, explicitly modeled relational warehouse transfers to heterogeneous unseen schemas, we evaluated the identical multi-stage pipeline on a small stratified transfer probe of \SpiderSampleQueries{} queries across \SpiderUniqueDatabases{} distinct SQLite databases from the public Spider benchmark \cite{yu2018spider} (Table~\ref{tab:spider_evaluation}). We emphasize that this 50-query evaluation serves as a transfer probe across 20 unseen databases, not a comprehensive evaluation on the entire 1,034-query Spider benchmark.

\IfFileExists{tables/tab_spider_evaluation.tex}{\input{tables/tab_spider_evaluation.tex}}{\input{../tables/tab_spider_evaluation.tex}}

Under zero-shot transfer, the system preserved execution reliability (100.0\% SQL Execution Success across all 20 external databases) but experienced a substantial decline in semantic equivalence, achieving \SpiderEquivalentAccuracy{} Result Equivalence (9/50 matches). This empirical result demonstrates that strong performance within an explicitly modeled enterprise data warehouse does not automatically transfer to heterogeneous, uncurated external schemas without database-specific catalog introspection and schema tuning. We intentionally report this as an empirical boundary of the architecture, adhering to the experimental stop-condition rather than re-engineering the warehouse pipeline into a generic schema linker.

\section{Limitations and Threats to Validity}
We explicitly document the scientific and operational limitations of this study:
\begin{enumerate}\sloppy
    \item \textbf{Single Primary Warehouse \& In-Domain Assumptions:} The primary 500-query benchmark is conducted on the Brazilian E-Commerce (Olist) data warehouse (9 tables, 100,000+ orders) with SQLite execution. Schema grounding assumptions tuned for this enterprise schema do not automatically translate to arbitrary domains.
    \item \textbf{Cross-Schema Transfer Gap (18.0\% Spider Result):} On the 20-database, 50-query Spider transfer probe, result equivalence dropped to 18.0\%, demonstrating a pronounced semantic-generalization gap on heterogeneous external schemas.
    \item \textbf{Sample Size of Transfer Probe:} The Spider transfer evaluation is a targeted 50-query stratified probe across 20 databases, not a full benchmark run.
    \item \textbf{Inference Latency Overhead:} Multi-stage retrieval, planning, validation, and verification incur a mean latency of \HeadlineMeanLatency{} ($p95$: \HeadlinePNinetyFiveLatency{}), making this architecture suited for asynchronous business intelligence rather than sub-second interactive querying.
    \item \textbf{Hard Query Complexity Ceiling:} Result equivalence drops to 44.55\% on hard queries and 32.56\% on complex aggregated tables, reflecting persistent challenges in multi-step CTE nesting and window functions.
    \item \textbf{Typographical Vulnerability:} The schema retriever degrades significantly under typographical perturbations (57.1\% retention), indicating the necessity of fuzzy edit-distance indexing.
    \item \textbf{False-Positive Repair Regressions:} Heuristic repair rules induced regressions in 22 out of 101 triggered cases in this evaluation setting, confirming that syntactic repair success is not equivalent to semantic recovery.
    \item \textbf{Empirical Comparator Scope:} The row-multiset comparator is an empirical evaluation criterion with numerical tolerance under the defined comparator, not a formal mathematical proof of semantic correctness.
    \item \textbf{Ablation Sample Sizes:} Component ablations ($N=100$) and synthetic perturbation tests ($N=50$) use smaller sample sizes than the main 500-query benchmark.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}
In this study, we investigated the architectural mechanisms governing the reliability of LLM-generated analytical SQL over a public relational e-commerce data warehouse. On an audited 500-query benchmark, our multi-stage pipeline achieved a \textbf{\HeadlineEquivalentAccuracy{} Result Equivalence Rate under the study comparator} and \textbf{\HeadlineSQLExecutionSuccess{} SQL Execution Success}. Our controlled component ablation demonstrated that adding AST-based structural verification provides a statistically significant improvement over unverified planning (Config~C 26.0\% vs.\ Config~B 15.0\%, exact $p=0.0192$, $\text{OR}=3.75$). However, the ablation does not establish that planning itself improves performance over basic RAG (Config~B 15.0\% vs.\ Config~A 19.0\%) or that the full system is causally superior. Furthermore, an exhaustive audit of 101 repair cases revealed that automated self-repair is a double-edged mechanism, producing \RepairHarmedFalsePositiveCount{} harmful false-positive regressions against only \RepairTrulyRecoveredCount{} genuine recoveries. We conclude that conservative, uncertainty-aware structural verification is preferable to unconstrained automated repair loops.
